title: YOU KEEP ASKING, “HOW FAR IS TOO FAR?” LOVE ASKS A DIFFERENT QUESTION.
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING, “HOW FAR IS TOO FAR?” LOVE ASKS A DIFFERENT QUESTION.
Maybe the most dangerous question in your Christian life isn't “Is this a sin?” Maybe it's “How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
There is a question Christians ask that sounds innocent.
Sometimes it even sounds spiritual.
“How far is too far?”
How far can we go physically before dating becomes sexual sin?
How much can I drink before I've crossed the line?
How explicit can the movie be before I shouldn't watch it?
How flirtatious can these messages become before I'm being unfaithful?
How much profanity, sexual content, violence, gossip, or darkness can I consume before it starts affecting my relationship with God?
Can Christians listen to this?
Can Christians wear that?
Can Christians go there?
Can Christians watch this?
Can Christians do what everybody else is doing if the Bible never specifically says, “Thou shalt not”?
And beneath all those questions there can sometimes be another question hiding.
A question we rarely say out loud.
Jesus, how much of the world can I keep without losing You?
That question hurts.
Because some of us recognize ourselves in it.
Maybe you have been trying to find the exact boundary.
Not because you hate Jesus.
You may genuinely love Him.
You pray.
You worship.
You read Scripture.
You may serve in church.
You may have cried during worship songs and meant every word.
But somewhere along the journey, discipleship quietly became negotiation.
You stopped asking, “Does this honor Christ?”
And started asking, “Can I get away with this?”
You stopped asking, “Will this make me more like Jesus?”
And started asking, “Where exactly does the Bible say I can't?”
You stopped asking, “Is this feeding my spirit?”
And started asking, “Is it technically sinful?”
And there is an enormous difference.
Because holiness was never supposed to be a game where we discover how close we can stand to the cliff without falling.
Jesus did not rescue you from darkness so you could spend the rest of your life measuring how close to darkness you are permitted to live.
Listen carefully to what Jesus actually said.
In John 14:15, the Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
“If you love Me, you will keep My commandments.”
The sentence is devastatingly simple.
Jesus brings obedience into the language of love.
The Greek verb ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate comes from agapaō, “to love.”
And τηρήσετε — tērēsete comes from tēreō, carrying the idea of keeping, observing, guarding, or holding fast.
Jesus isn't describing salvation as something we purchase through flawless moral performance.
That would contradict the Gospel.
We are not saved because we behaved well enough.
We are saved by grace.
We are reconciled to God through Christ.
Jesus lived the righteousness we could not produce, bore sin at the cross, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not wages paid to impressive Christians. It is grace received through faith.
But grace does something to the heart.
When you begin to understand what Christ has done for you, obedience stops looking merely like God taking things away from you.
It starts looking like love responding to Love.
That changes the question.
Imagine a husband asking:
“How romantic can I become with another woman before it technically counts as cheating?”
Something already feels wrong, doesn't it?
Even before an affair happens, the question reveals something troubling about the direction of his desire.
A faithful husband doesn't normally wake up thinking:
“What is the maximum amount of intimacy I can give another woman while still technically remaining faithful to my wife?”
Love asks something else.
“How can I honor the person I love?”
And perhaps that is the question some of us desperately need to recover with Jesus.
Not:
How far is too far?
But:
How close can I walk with Christ?
That changes dating.
Instead of asking, “How much physical intimacy can we get away with before God calls it sexual immorality?”
You begin asking:
“How can this relationship help both of us honor Jesus?”
“How can I protect this person's heart instead of using their body to satisfy my desires?”
“How can our relationship make holiness easier rather than temptation stronger?”
Suddenly the person sitting beside you isn't merely somebody you're attracted to.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
Someone Christ commands you to love.
Someone whose body isn't your property.
Someone whose soul matters more than tonight's chemistry.
And yes, sometimes that means boundaries.
Real ones.
Not because bodies are evil.
Christianity teaches something far more beautiful.
Your body matters to God.
Paul told believers that their bodies were members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit, then said:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6.
And notice the language surrounding Paul's argument.
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει.
“All things are lawful for me,” Paul writes, “but not all things are helpful.”
Then comes another piercing statement:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
That reaches far beyond dating.
Because sometimes the question isn't simply:
“Am I allowed to do this?”
Sometimes the better question is:
“What is this doing to me?”
You say you can stop watching whenever you want.
Can you?
You say those videos don't affect your mind.
Are you sure?
You say the music doesn't shape you.
You say the jokes don't matter.
You say the private messages are innocent.
You say nobody knows about the pornography.
You say the flirting is harmless.
You say the drinking is under control.
You say scrolling for three hours every night isn't an addiction.
You say you aren't compromising.
But perhaps there is another question worth asking.
Is it mastering you?
Because something doesn't have to put handcuffs around your wrists to become your master.
Sometimes slavery arrives through a screen.
Sometimes it arrives through loneliness.
Sometimes it looks like validation.
Sometimes it sounds like:
“Everybody does it.”
Sometimes it whispers:
“Just one more time.”
And eventually you realize you have spent months asking God to bless a life you keep designing around the very things weakening your hunger for Him.
That realization can sting.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Gospel does not expose your darkness so Jesus can humiliate you.
Jesus brings darkness into the light because He intends to free you.
Maybe you've already gone farther than you ever thought you would.
Maybe you crossed the boundary.
Maybe several boundaries.
Maybe you're reading this thinking:
This article would have helped me three years ago.
Maybe you slept with someone you weren't married to.
Maybe pornography rewired parts of your imagination.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you sent the pictures.
Maybe you became the person you once promised yourself you would never become.
Maybe the relationship you defended eventually broke you.
Maybe nobody at church knows.
Maybe your parents don't know.
Maybe your spouse doesn't know.
Maybe the people who see you worship on Sunday would never imagine what you fight on Tuesday night.
And now shame tells you that articles about holiness are for people who haven't ruined theirs.
No.
Look at Jesus.
The Gospel is not:
“Keep yourself clean enough so Jesus will want you.”
The Gospel is:
You could not cleanse yourself, so Christ came for sinners.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride dies because you cannot save yourself.
Despair dies because your sin is not greater than the sufficiency of Christ.
You don't need to pretend you never crossed the line.
You need to bring your sin to the One who crossed heaven and earth to redeem sinners.
Repentance isn't merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
Repentance turns.
It comes into the light.
It stops defending what God calls sin.
It stops negotiating.
It says:
“Jesus, I was wrong.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I don't want to keep living divided.”
And grace meets you there.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that says sin doesn't matter.
Grace that paid an unimaginable price because sin mattered so much.
The blood of Jesus was not spilled so we could become comfortable with the chains He died to break.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace picks up ruined people and begins rewriting stories.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
Maybe your story has chapters you wish you could tear out.
Jesus knows.
Maybe your search history has chapters.
Your dating history.
Your sexual history.
Your thought life.
Your addictions.
Your compromises.
Your secret conversations.
Your repeated apologies to God.
Your “last times” that weren't actually the last time.
He knows.
And still the invitation of Christ is not:
“Hide better.”
It is:
Come into the light.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new way to live.
And once you understand that, holiness stops being an audition for God's affection.
You aren't obeying so Jesus will finally love you.
You begin obeying because in Christ you have encountered a love so costly that compromise starts losing some of its beauty.
This is why the Christian question cannot always stop at:
“Is it allowed?”
Paul gives another breathtaking principle in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε.
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”
Even eating.
Even drinking.
Even ordinary life.
πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ — panta eis doxan theou.
Everything toward the glory of God.
That is a radically different compass.
Before watching it:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Before sending it:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Before dating them:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Before going back to that website:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Before entering that conversation:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Before putting your body into that situation:
“Can I glorify God here?”
Not:
“How close can I get?”
But:
“Where is Jesus leading me?”
And sometimes faithful Christians will reach different conclusions in matters where Scripture gives no explicit prohibition.
That matters.
We must never turn personal preferences into commandments God never gave.
Christian holiness is not legalism.
Not every movie is sinful because one Christian cannot watch it.
Not every cultural preference is biblical law.
Not every disputed matter has a verse providing an exact boundary.
Scripture itself recognizes matters of conscience.
So this isn't an invitation to become suspicious of everything enjoyable.
It isn't permission to police everyone else's conscience.
And it certainly isn't permission to create extra-biblical commandments and then measure everyone's Christianity by them.
It is something much more personal.
What does your desire reveal about your heart?
Because sometimes we spend enormous energy looking for loopholes when we already know what the Holy Spirit has been confronting.
You didn't really need another debate.
You needed surrender.
You already knew that relationship was pulling you away.
You already knew those messages needed to stop.
You already knew you needed accountability.
You already knew what happened every time you watched that kind of content alone.
You already knew that environment consistently weakened your resistance.
But you kept asking:
“How far is too far?”
Maybe because you wanted someone to move the line.
And Jesus keeps bringing you back to Himself.
“If you love Me…”
There it is.
Not merely the boundary.
The Person.
Christianity isn't ultimately about falling in love with rules.
It is about Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who ate with outcasts.
The One who told the truth when the truth hurt.
The One betrayed for silver.
The One mocked.
The One beaten.
The One crowned with thorns.
The One nailed to wood.
The One who prayed for His enemies.
The One who died.
The One whose tomb could not hold Him.
Jesus Christ.
And when that Jesus becomes more precious to you, holiness begins to change shape.
It isn't:
“How much pleasure must I surrender?”
It becomes:
“Why would I trade intimacy with Christ for something that keeps leaving me emptier?”
That doesn't mean temptation disappears.
Some nights you will still want what you know isn't good for you.
Some relationships will still be difficult to leave.
Some habits will require accountability, confession, radical boundaries, pastoral help, and perhaps professional help where addiction or serious mental-health concerns are involved.
Some battles won't end after one emotional prayer.
Sanctification is often slower than the testimony videos make it appear.
But struggling against sin is different from making peace with it.
You can stumble while walking toward Jesus.
The danger is when you rearrange the road so you no longer have to call the stumbling “stumbling.”
Don't rename bondage freedom.
Don't rename lust love.
Don't rename compromise maturity.
Don't rename conviction legalism merely because conviction is uncomfortable.
And don't rename shame repentance either.
Jesus isn't asking you to spend the rest of your life staring backward at everything you've done.
He calls you forward.
Perhaps tonight your prayer doesn't need impressive theology.
Maybe it simply needs honesty.
“Jesus, I have been asking how much I can keep.”
“I've been negotiating.”
“I've defended things because I didn't want to surrender them.”
“I've called things freedom that have quietly become masters.”
“Forgive me.”
“Teach me to love You more than the compromise.”
“Teach me to want what honors You.”
That prayer can become the beginning of something.
And if this exposed something you've been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail.
But don't keep pretending.
Somebody reading the comments may realize they aren't the only Christian fighting this battle.
Somebody may find courage because you were honest first.
And there is probably someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message tonight.
Maybe your son.
Your daughter.
Your boyfriend.
Your girlfriend.
Your friend who keeps getting pulled back into the same relationship.
The teenager trying to follow Jesus while everyone around them calls holiness outdated.
The believer secretly wondering whether surrender is worth it.
The person who hasn't entered a church in years.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.
But if this truth helped you, helping carry biblical truth to another person can be one practical way to use what God has placed in your hands for His glory.
If you believe this work should continue reaching people, supporting it is one practical opportunity to participate. Our salvation rests in Christ alone.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer becoming spiritually numb.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Even invite the person who doesn't believe yet.
Let them encounter Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is still staring at a boundary.
Still calculating.
Still bargaining.
Still asking:
“How far can I go?”
And perhaps what they desperately need isn't another centimeter marked on the line.
Perhaps they need to look away from the line…
and look at Christ.
The question was never merely how close you could stand to sin without crossing over.
The deeper question is whether Jesus has become precious enough that you no longer want your entire Christian life to be spent standing at the border.
You were called closer.
Closer to Christ.
Closer to truth.
Closer to freedom.
Closer to the One who loved you all the way to the cross.
So when temptation whispers tomorrow:
“How far is too far?”
Remember the question love learned to ask instead:
“Jesus, what would honor You?”
And follow Him from there.
One day you may realize the boundary you were afraid would cost you your freedom was actually Jesus leading you out of your chains.
